blocks.html: In precalculus you used proof by induction to prove formulas for sums. Induction proves much more: divisibility facts, inequalities, statements about all sizes of objects. The structure stays the same; what changes is the inductive step, which becomes a small direct proof in which the case $n = k$ must actually be used.

To prove $P(n)$ for every integer $n \ge n_{0}$: (1) base case, prove $P(n_{0})$; (2) inductive step, assume $P(k)$ for some $k \ge n_{0}$ (the inductive hypothesis) and prove $P(k + 1)$. The step works by rewriting the case $k + 1$ so that the case $k$ appears inside it.

The base case knocks over the first domino, and the step guarantees each domino knocks over the next: $P(n_{0})$ gives $P(n_{0} + 1)$, which gives $P(n_{0} + 2)$, and so on forever. Two things can go wrong. If the step never uses $P(k)$, it is really a direct proof in disguise or, more often, it has a gap. And if the base case is checked where the claim is false, nothing gets started; an inequality like $2^{n} > n^{2}$ must start where it really begins to hold.

head: $n$
blocks.cap: Where does $2^{n} > n^{2}$ start?

blocks.title: A divisibility proof
blocks.q: Prove that $3 \mid 4^{n} - 1$ for every integer $n \ge 1$.
steps: Base case $n = 1$: $4 - 1 = 3$, which is divisible by $3$.
Inductive step: assume $3 \mid 4^{k} - 1$, say $4^{k} - 1 = 3m$.
Rewrite the next case to contain the old one: $4^{k+1} - 1 = 4 \cdot 4^{k} - 1 = 4(4^{k} - 1) + 3$.
Substitute: $4(3m) + 3 = 3(4m + 1)$, a multiple of $3$. So the claim holds for every $n \ge 1$.

blocks.title: An inequality with a late start
blocks.q: Prove that $2^{n} > n^{2}$ for every integer $n \ge 5$.
steps: Base case $n = 5$: $32 > 25$. (The table shows why we cannot start lower: it fails at $2$, $3$ and $4$.)
Step: assume $2^{k} > k^{2}$ with $k \ge 5$. Then $2^{k+1} = 2 \cdot 2^{k} > 2k^{2}$.
It remains to show $2k^{2} \ge (k + 1)^{2}$, that is, $k^{2} \ge 2k + 1$, or $(k - 1)^{2} \ge 2$. That holds for every $k \ge 3$, so certainly for $k \ge 5$.

blocks.title: Factorials outgrow powers
blocks.q: Prove that $n! > 2^{n}$ for every integer $n \ge 4$.
steps: Base case $n = 4$: $24 > 16$.
Step: assume $k! > 2^{k}$ with $k \ge 4$. Then $(k + 1)! = (k + 1) \cdot k! > (k + 1) \cdot 2^{k}$.
Since $k + 1 \ge 5 > 2$, this is more than $2 \cdot 2^{k} = 2^{k+1}$.

blocks.html: Starting at the wrong base case, or never using $P(k)$. A "proof" of $2^{n} > n^{2}$ that checks $n = 1$ and then runs the step has a hidden flaw: the step needed $k \ge 3$, and the claim is false at $n = 2, 3, 4$. And a step that proves $P(k + 1)$ from scratch, without the hypothesis, has usually skipped something. Check: test the claim at the first few values to find where it truly starts, and point to the line of the step where $P(k)$ is used.

blocks.html: In ordinary induction each case leans on the one just before it. Some arguments need to reach further back: a number splits into two smaller factors, or an amount of postage is a smaller amount plus one stamp. Strong induction allows exactly that.

Strong induction: to prove $P(n)$ for all $n \ge n_{0}$, prove the base cases, then show that if $P(n_{0}), P(n_{0} + 1), \ldots, P(k)$ are all true, so is $P(k + 1)$. If the step uses the case $k + 1 - j$, you need $j$ consecutive base cases, because the first $j$ values have nothing to step from.

Strong induction is no stronger than ordinary induction (each can be turned into the other), but it fits problems where case $k + 1$ depends on an earlier case that is not $k$. The base cases matter more: if the step reaches back $4$ places, it builds case $16$ from case $12$, case $17$ from $13$, and so on. Unless all four of $12$, $13$, $14$, $15$ are checked directly, some chain of cases never gets started.

blocks.title: Postage with 4¢ and 5¢ stamps
blocks.q: Prove that every amount of at least 12¢ can be paid with 4¢ and 5¢ stamps.
steps: Step: let $n \ge 16$ and assume every amount from $12$ to $n - 1$ can be paid. Then $n - 4 \ge 12$ can be paid; add one 4¢ stamp to pay $n$.
The step reaches back $4$, which is why exactly four base cases were needed. (And $11$¢ really is impossible, so $12$ is the right start.)

blocks.title: Products of primes
blocks.q: Prove that every integer $n \ge 2$ is a prime or a product of primes.
steps: Base case: $2$ is prime.
Step: assume every integer from $2$ to $k$ is a prime or a product of primes, and look at $k + 1$.
If $k + 1$ is prime, done. Otherwise $k + 1 = ab$ with $2 \le a, b \le k$. By the hypothesis, $a$ and $b$ are products of primes, so $ab$ is too.
Ordinary induction would not help: knowing about $k$ says nothing about $k + 1$'s factors, which can be any smaller numbers.
blocks.a: Split $k + 1 = ab$ and apply the hypothesis to both factors.

blocks.title: A sequence with two base cases
steps: Base cases: $a_{1} = 1 < 2$ and $a_{2} = 3 < 4$. Two are needed because the step uses two earlier terms.
Step: for $k + 1 \ge 3$, assume the claim for all smaller indices. Then $a_{k+1} = a_{k} + a_{k-1} < 2^{k} + 2^{k-1} < 2^{k} + 2^{k} = 2^{k+1}$.

blocks.html: Checking one base case when the step reaches further back. For the postage problem, checking only $12$ and stepping from $n - 4$ proves $16, 20, 24, \ldots$ and nothing about $13$ or $17$. Check: if the step uses the case $j$ places back, verify $j$ consecutive starting cases.

blocks.html: In algebra you met recursive formulas given to you. Here you build them. Many counting problems are hard to attack head-on but easy once you notice that a big object is a small object with one more piece. That is the sum rule again, and strong induction is what makes the recurrence trustworthy.

To set up a recurrence for $a_{n}$, split the objects of size $n$ by how they end (their last piece). Each case should leave a smaller object of the same kind, counted by an earlier term. Add the cases, and state enough starting values for the recurrence to run.

Take tilings of a 1-by-$n$ strip with squares and dominoes. The last tile is either a square, leaving a strip of length $n - 1$ tiled in any of $a_{n-1}$ ways, or a domino, leaving length $n - 2$ in $a_{n-2}$ ways. These cases cannot overlap and cover everything, so $a_{n} = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}$. Since the recurrence reaches back two steps, it needs two starting values: $a_{1} = 1$ and $a_{2} = 2$.

blocks.name: disc-tiling
blocks.cap: Every tiling sorted by its last tile. Each group is a complete list of smaller tilings, so the counts add: $a_{n} = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}$. Move the slider to grow $n$.

blocks.title: Tilings
blocks.q: How many ways are there to tile a 1-by-$6$ strip with squares and dominoes?

blocks.title: Strings with no two 1s in a row
blocks.q: Let $b_{n}$ count bit strings of length $n$ with no two 1s next to each other. Set up a recurrence and find $b_{5}$.
steps: Split by the end. If the string ends in 0, the first $n - 1$ bits can be any good string: $b_{n-1}$.
If it ends in 1, the bit before must be 0, so it ends in 01, and the first $n - 2$ bits can be any good string: $b_{n-2}$.

blocks.title: The Tower of Hanoi
blocks.q: Disks of $n$ sizes sit on a peg, largest at the bottom. Move them to another peg, one at a time, never putting a disk on a smaller one. Find a recurrence for the fewest moves $h_{n}$.
steps: The largest disk must move at some point, and when it does, the other $n - 1$ disks must all be on the third peg.
So: move $n - 1$ disks out of the way ($h_{n-1}$ moves), move the largest ($1$), then move the $n - 1$ disks on top of it ($h_{n-1}$).

blocks.name: disc-tiling
blocks.cap: The Tower of Hanoi: step through the best solution and watch the three phases.

blocks.html: Missing a way the pattern can end, or forgetting starting values. Counting only tilings that end in a square gives $a_{n} = a_{n-1}$, which says every length has just one tiling. And $a_{n} = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}$ alone does not determine a sequence: with $a_{1} = 2$, $a_{2} = 3$ you get the bit strings, not the tilings. Check: list all cases for small $n$ by hand and make sure the recurrence reproduces them.

blocks.html: A recurrence tells you how to get the next term, but computing $a_{100}$ step by step is slow. A closed form gives $a_{n}$ directly. For many first-order recurrences you can find one by substituting the rule into itself and recognizing a sum, often a geometric series.

To unroll $a_{n} = c\,a_{n-1} + d$: replace $a_{n-1}$ by $c\,a_{n-2} + d$, then $a_{n-2}$ by $c\,a_{n-3} + d$, and so on, until the pattern is clear and you reach the starting value. Then check the closed form by substituting it into the recurrence and the starting value (an induction proof).

Each substitution pushes the index down by one and adds one more term to a growing sum. After $j$ steps, $a_{n} = c^{j}a_{n-j} + d(c^{j-1} + \cdots + c + 1)$. Going all the way to the start turns the sum into a geometric series with a known total. The check matters because "the pattern is clear" is a guess until it is verified; unrolling suggests the answer, and induction confirms it.

blocks.title: The Tower of Hanoi, solved
steps: The geometric sum is $2^{n} - 1$.
Check: $h_{1} = 2 - 1 = 1$, and $2(2^{n-1} - 1) + 1 = 2^{n} - 1$. It satisfies both.

blocks.title: Adding $n$ each time
blocks.q: Solve $a_{n} = a_{n-1} + n$ with $a_{0} = 0$.
steps: Unroll: $a_{n} = a_{n-2} + (n - 1) + n = \cdots = a_{0} + 1 + 2 + \cdots + n$.

blocks.html: A shortcut for $a_{n} = c\,a_{n-1} + d$ with $c \ne 1$: find the fixed point $p$ with $p = cp + d$, so $p = \frac{d}{1 - c}$. Subtracting $p = cp + d$ from the recurrence gives $a_{n} - p = c(a_{n-1} - p)$: the distance from $p$ is multiplied by $c$ each step. So $a_{n} = p + c^{n}(a_{0} - p)$. In the last example $p = 2$ and $a_{0} - p = 3$, giving $2 + 3 \cdot 3^{n}$ again.

Guessing a formula from the first two terms and never checking it. Hanoi starts $1, 3$, which fits $2n - 1$; but the next term is $7$, not $5$. Two terms fit a straight line through them, whatever the sequence really is. Check: compute a third term (or more) from the recurrence, and substitute your formula into the recurrence itself.

sources.name: Oscar Levin, Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction (3rd ed.), section "Solving Recurrence Relations" (iteration)
MIT OpenCourseWare 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science (Lehman, Leighton and Meyer), chapter "Recurrences" (plug and chug)

blocks.html: Unrolling works when each term depends on one earlier term. Recurrences like $a_{n} = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}$ reach back two steps, and unrolling gets messy. Instead we guess the shape of the answer, and the guess reduces to a quadratic equation, solved with the quadratic formula or by factoring. It is the systematic follow-up to unrolling.

For $a_{n} = c_{1}a_{n-1} + c_{2}a_{n-2}$, solve the characteristic equation $r^{2} = c_{1}r + c_{2}$. If its roots $r_{1} \ne r_{2}$, every solution is $a_{n} = A\,r_{1}^{n} + B\,r_{2}^{n}$; find $A$ and $B$ from the two starting values.

Try $a_{n} = r^{n}$. Substituting gives $r^{n} = c_{1}r^{n-1} + c_{2}r^{n-2}$; dividing by $r^{n-2}$ leaves $r^{2} = c_{1}r + c_{2}$. So $r^{n}$ is a solution exactly when $r$ is a root. The recurrence is linear, so any combination $Ar_{1}^{n} + Br_{2}^{n}$ of two solutions is again a solution. Two free constants can match any two starting values (the equations $A + B = a_{0}$, $Ar_{1} + Br_{2} = a_{1}$ have a solution when $r_{1} \ne r_{2}$), and two starting values determine the whole sequence.

blocks.name: disc-tiling
blocks.cap: Domino tilings grow like the Fibonacci numbers. The ratio column approaches the larger characteristic root of $r^{2} = r + 1$, the golden ratio $\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$.

blocks.title: Two whole-number roots
steps: Characteristic equation: $r^{2} = 5r - 6$, so $r^{2} - 5r + 6 = 0 = (r - 2)(r - 3)$: roots $2$ and $3$.
$a_{n} = A \cdot 2^{n} + B \cdot 3^{n}$. From $n = 0$: $A + B = 1$. From $n = 1$: $2A + 3B = 4$.
Subtract twice the first equation from the second: $B = 2$, so $A = -1$.
$a_{n} = 2 \cdot 3^{n} - 2^{n}$. Check $a_{2}$: the formula gives $18 - 4 = 14$; the recurrence gives $5 \cdot 4 - 6 \cdot 1 = 14$.

blocks.title: A negative root
steps: $A + B = 2$ and $2A - B = 1$. Adding: $3A = 3$, so $A = 1$ and $B = 1$.
$a_{n} = 2^{n} + (-1)^{n}$: $2, 1, 5, 7, 17, \ldots$, which matches the recurrence.

blocks.title: The Fibonacci numbers
blocks.q: What does this method give for $F_{n} = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$, $F_{0} = 0$, $F_{1} = 1$?
steps: $r^{2} = r + 1$ has roots $\varphi = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ and $\psi = \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}$.
Fitting $A + B = 0$ and $A\varphi + B\psi = 1$ gives $A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$, $B = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$.
So $F_{n} = \dfrac{\varphi^{n} - \psi^{n}}{\sqrt{5}}$ (Binet's formula). Since $|\psi| < 1$, $F_{n}$ is the whole number nearest $\varphi^{n}/\sqrt{5}$.

blocks.html: Wrong signs in the characteristic equation, or fitting only one starting value. For $a_{n} = 5a_{n-1} - 6a_{n-2}$ the equation is $r^{2} - 5r + 6 = 0$, not $r^{2} + 5r - 6 = 0$: move the terms across the equals sign and their signs change. And $A$ and $B$ need both $a_{0}$ and $a_{1}$; a formula fitted to $a_{0}$ alone is just a guess. Check: compute $a_{2}$ from your formula and from the recurrence.

blocks.html: The method for linear recurrences needs two different roots to make two different solutions. When the characteristic equation is a perfect square, there is only one root, and we need a second solution from somewhere else.
If $r^{2} = c_{1}r + c_{2}$ has a double root $r$ (so $c_{1} = 2r$ and $c_{2} = -r^{2}$), then every solution of $a_{n} = c_{1}a_{n-1} + c_{2}a_{n-2}$ has the form $$a_{n} = (A + Bn)\,r^{n}.$$

Check that $n r^{n}$ is a solution. With $c_{1} = 2r$ and $c_{2} = -r^{2}$: $$c_{1}(n - 1)r^{n-1} + c_{2}(n - 2)r^{n-2} = 2(n - 1)r^{n} - (n - 2)r^{n} = n r^{n}.$$ So both $r^{n}$ and $n r^{n}$ solve the recurrence, and so does $A r^{n} + B n r^{n}$. Two free constants match two starting values: $n = 0$ gives $A = a_{0}$, and $n = 1$ gives $(A + B)r = a_{1}$.

blocks.title: A double root of $3$
steps: $a_{n} = (1 + n)3^{n}$. Check $a_{2}$: $3 \cdot 9 = 27$ from the formula, $6 \cdot 6 - 9 \cdot 1 = 27$ from the recurrence.

blocks.title: Using the closed form
blocks.q: For $a_{n} = -6a_{n-1} - 9a_{n-2}$ with $a_{0} = 1$, $a_{1} = -6$, find $a_{4}$ from a closed form.

blocks.html: Where does the extra $n$ come from? If the two roots were $r$ and a nearby $s$, the combination $\frac{s^{n} - r^{n}}{s - r}$ would be a solution. As $s$ approaches $r$, this tends to the derivative of $x^{n}$ at $r$, which is $n r^{n-1}$, a constant times $n r^{n}$. The repeated root case is the limit of the distinct root case.

Writing $A \cdot r^{n} + B \cdot r^{n}$. That is just $(A + B)r^{n}$, one solution with one constant, and it forces $a_{1} = r\,a_{0}$. In the first example it would need $a_{1} = 3$, but $a_{1} = 6$. Check: your general solution must have two different pieces, neither a multiple of the other; for a double root the second piece carries the extra factor $n$.

blocks.html: When we compare algorithms, or counts like $2^{n}$ and $n!$, we care about what happens as $n$ grows, not about small cases or constant factors. Big-O notation makes that precise, and its definition is a nested quantifier statement. Logarithms, which grow slowly, sit at the bottom of the growth ladder.

$f$ is $O(g)$ ("big-O of $g$") when there are constants $C$ and $k$ such that $|f(n)| \le C\,|g(n)|$ for every $n > k$. The common growth classes, from slowest to fastest, are $$\log n \ll \sqrt{n} \ll n \ll n\log n \ll n^{2} \ll n^{3} \ll 2^{n} \ll n!.$$

Read the definition with its quantifiers: there exist $C$ and $k$ such that for all $n > k$… The "for all $n > k$" ignores any finite beginning, and the $C$ absorbs constant factors. So $100n$ is $O(n)$ (take $C = 100$), and $n^{2}$ is not $O(100n)$: whatever $C$ you pick, $n^{2} \le 100Cn$ fails once $n > 100C$. For the ladder, compare ratios: $n^{2}/n = n$ grows without bound, so $n^{2}$ is not $O(n)$, and the same argument works for each step up.

blocks.title: A constant cannot rescue it
steps: Suppose $n^{2} \le C \cdot 100n$ for all $n > k$. Dividing by $n$: $n \le 100C$ for all $n > k$.
That fails for any $n$ larger than both $k$ and $100C$.
So no $C$ works: $n^{2}$ is not $O(100n)$, even though $100n$ is the larger one for every $n < 100$.

blocks.title: The tightest class
blocks.q: Let $f(n) = 5n\log_{2} n + 100n + 7$. Which is the slowest-growing of $n$, $n\log n$, $n^{2}$ that $f$ is big-O of?
steps: The term $5n\log_{2} n$ eventually dominates: $100n \le 100\,n\log_{2} n$ once $\log_{2} n \ge 1$, and $7 \le 7n\log_{2} n$ too.
So $f(n) \le 112\,n\log_{2} n$ for $n \ge 2$: $f$ is $O(n\log n)$. It is also $O(n^{2})$, but that is a looser statement. It is not $O(n)$, since $f(n)/n \ge 5\log_{2} n$ is unbounded.

blocks.html: Judging growth from small values, or thinking a constant changes the class. At $n = 50$, $100n = 5{,}000$ beats $n^{2} = 2{,}500$, but that says nothing about large $n$. And $1000n$ and $n$ are both $O(n)$: big-O deliberately ignores constant factors. Check: look at the ratio $f(n)/g(n)$ for large $n$. If it stays bounded, $f$ is $O(g)$; if it grows without bound, it is not.

blocks.html: Road maps, friendships, computer networks and molecules all have the same skeleton: things, and connections between pairs of them. A graph is that skeleton. It is built from sets, and its first theorem is a counting argument in the spirit of the sum rule.

A graph $G = (V, E)$ has a set $V$ of vertices and a set $E$ of edges, each edge joining two different vertices (on this site graphs are simple: no loops, no repeated edges, unless a problem says otherwise). The degree $\deg(v)$ of a vertex is the number of edges touching it. Handshake lemma: $$\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|.$$

Count the pairs (vertex, edge touching it) in two ways. Going vertex by vertex, there are $\deg(v)$ pairs for each $v$, so the total is the sum of the degrees. Going edge by edge, each edge touches exactly two vertices, so the total is $2|E|$. Same pairs, two counts, equal totals. A consequence: the sum of the degrees is even, so the number of vertices with odd degree must be even.

blocks.title: Edges from degrees
blocks.q: A graph has degree sequence $3, 3, 2, 2, 2$. How many edges does it have?
steps: Sum of degrees: $3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12$.
Handshake lemma: $2|E| = 12$, so $|E| = 6$.

blocks.title: An impossible graph
blocks.q: Can a graph have degrees $3, 3, 3, 2, 2$?
steps: The degrees add to $13$, an odd number.
But the sum must be $2|E|$, which is even. So no graph has these degrees.
Equivalently: it would have three vertices of odd degree, and the number of odd-degree vertices is always even.

blocks.title: A handshake puzzle
blocks.q: At a party of $9$ people, can everyone shake hands with exactly $3$ others?
steps: Make a graph: people are vertices, handshakes are edges. Each vertex would have degree $3$.
The degree sum would be $9 \cdot 3 = 27$, which is odd, but it must equal twice the number of handshakes.
So it is impossible. (With $10$ people it is possible: the sum is $30$, for $15$ handshakes.)

blocks.html: Believing a graph can have an odd number of odd-degree vertices. When building examples, it is easy to write down degrees like $3, 2, 2, 2$ and look for a graph. None exists: the sum $9$ is odd. Check: add the degrees first; if the total is odd, stop.
The degree sequence lists the degrees from largest to smallest. Two very different-looking drawings can have the same degree sequence; a drawing is just one picture of a graph.

blocks.html: A few graphs come up so often that they have names. Knowing their edge counts and degrees saves time, and each count is a small exercise in the handshake lemma or in combinations.

The complete graph $K_{n}$ joins every pair of its $n$ vertices: $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ edges, every degree $n - 1$. The complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$ has two sides of $m$ and $n$ vertices, with every vertex joined to every vertex on the other side and none on its own: $mn$ edges. The cycle $C_{n}$ ($n \ge 3$) is a ring of $n$ vertices with $n$ edges; the path $P_{n}$ is $n$ vertices in a row with $n - 1$ edges.

An edge of $K_{n}$ is a choice of two endpoints, so there are $\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ of them. The handshake lemma agrees: $n$ vertices of degree $n - 1$ give a degree sum of $n(n - 1)$, which is twice the number of edges. In $K_{m,n}$ an edge is one choice from each side, so the product rule gives $mn$.

blocks.html: Graphs model routes, so we need words for routes. The words differ in what may repeat, and the differences matter in every later topic, from Euler circuits to shortest paths. Everything is built on the vertices and edges of graph basics.

A walk is a sequence of vertices, each joined to the next by an edge; anything may repeat. A trail is a walk with no repeated edge. A path is a walk with no repeated vertex. A cycle is a closed trail (it ends where it starts) with no repeated vertex except that start and end. A graph is connected when every two vertices are joined by a path; its maximal connected pieces are its components.

Why does it not matter whether "connected" is defined with walks or with paths? Any walk from $u$ to $v$ contains a path from $u$ to $v$: if some vertex repeats, cut out the detour between its two visits, and repeat until no vertex repeats. The result is shorter and still goes from $u$ to $v$. So "joined by a walk" and "joined by a path" mean the same thing, and the shortest route between two vertices is always a path.

steps: $\{A, B, C\}$ are joined. $\{D, E\}$ are joined. $F$ and $G$ have no edges.
Each isolated vertex is a component by itself: $\{A, B, C\}$, $\{D, E\}$, $\{F\}$, $\{G\}$.

blocks.html: Mixing up walks, trails and paths. A route that passes through a crossroads twice is a trail, not a path, as long as it never reuses a road. And a walk that runs back and forth along one edge is not a trail. Check: first look for a repeated edge (then it is only a walk), then a repeated vertex (then it is a trail, not a path).
At least $n - 1$ edges are needed to connect $n$ vertices: each edge joins at most two components into one, and you start with $n$ separate vertices.

blocks.html: A computer stores a graph as a table of zeros and ones. That table, a matrix, does more than store: matrix multiplication turns out to count routes through the graph. This uses the walks from connectivity and the named graphs from special graphs.

For a graph with vertices $1, \ldots, n$, the adjacency matrix $A$ has entry $A_{ij} = 1$ when $i$ and $j$ are joined and $0$ otherwise. It is symmetric, its diagonal is $0$, and row $i$ adds up to $\deg(i)$. The $(i, j)$ entry of $A^{k}$ is the number of walks of length $k$ from $i$ to $j$.

Look at $A^{2}$: $(A^{2})_{ij} = \sum_{m} A_{im}A_{mj}$. A term is $1$ exactly when $m$ is joined to both $i$ and $j$, that is, when $i \to m \to j$ is a walk of length $2$. So the sum counts those walks, one per middle vertex. The same idea extends: $(A^{k+1})_{ij} = \sum_{m} (A^{k})_{im}A_{mj}$ counts walks of length $k$ from $i$ to some $m$, followed by one more step to $j$, and induction gives the result for every $k$.

steps: A diagonal entry $(A^{3})_{ii}$ counts closed walks of length $3$ from $i$; in a simple graph each one goes around a triangle.
One triangle $\{a, b, c\}$ produces $6$ such walks: $3$ starting points times $2$ directions.
So the diagonal sum is $6$ times the number of triangles.

blocks.html: The same graph can be drawn in many ways, with different labels. When are two graphs "really the same"? The answer uses a bijection between their vertex sets, and the named graphs from special graphs give good test cases.

Graphs $G$ and $H$ are isomorphic when there is a bijection $f : V(G) \to V(H)$ such that $u$ and $v$ are joined in $G$ exactly when $f(u)$ and $f(v)$ are joined in $H$. Properties preserved by every isomorphism are invariants: the number of vertices and edges, the degree sequence, connectedness, the number of triangles, the lengths of cycles. Different invariants prove two graphs are not isomorphic; matching invariants do not prove they are.

An isomorphism is a relabeling: rename each vertex $u$ of $G$ as $f(u)$, and the edge set becomes exactly the edge set of $H$. Anything defined only from vertices and edges, without looking at the names or the drawing, survives a relabeling. That is why invariants can rule isomorphism out. But many different graphs share all the simple invariants, so to show two graphs are isomorphic you have to produce the bijection.

Check every edge: $AB \mapsto 13$, $BC \mapsto 35$, $CD \mapsto 52$, $DE \mapsto 24$, $EA \mapsto 41$. All are edges of $H$.

blocks.html: In 1736 the people of Königsberg asked whether they could walk across each of their seven bridges exactly once. Euler answered with an argument about degrees, and graph theory began. The question is about trails: routes that never reuse an edge.

An Euler circuit is a closed trail that uses every edge exactly once; an Euler path uses every edge exactly once but may end somewhere else. A connected graph has an Euler circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree, and an Euler path (but no circuit) exactly when exactly two vertices have odd degree; the path must start at one of them and end at the other.

Each time a trail passes through a vertex, it arrives on one edge and leaves on another, using up two edges there. So at every vertex other than the start and end, the edges come in pairs: the degree is even. In a closed trail the start is also passed through, so every degree is even. For a path, the start and end each have one unpaired edge, so they, and only they, have odd degree. The converse (even degrees really do guarantee a circuit in a connected graph) is proved by building the circuit: start anywhere, walk until you return, and splice in detours through any unused edges.

blocks.html: Euler circuits use every edge once, and a quick degree count decides whether one exists. Ask instead for a route that visits every vertex once, and everything changes: no quick test is known, only good sufficient conditions and good reasons for failure.

A Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once; a Hamilton cycle also returns to its start. Dirac's theorem: if a simple graph has $n \ge 3$ vertices and every vertex has degree at least $n/2$, it has a Hamilton cycle. The condition is sufficient, not necessary.

Why can't we just count degrees as for Euler? A Hamilton cycle is a global object: whether one exists depends on how the whole graph fits together, not on each vertex separately. Some local facts do block it. A vertex of degree $1$ cannot be inside a cycle. If removing one vertex splits the graph, a cycle through everything would need to pass through that vertex twice. In a bipartite graph a cycle alternates sides, so the two sides must have equal size. Dirac's theorem works in the other direction: with that many edges at every vertex, there is always room to reroute and close a cycle.

blocks.html: Trees are the leanest connected graphs: family trees, file folders, the branches of a decision. Using paths and connectedness, they have several equivalent definitions, and one tidy count.

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. For a graph with $n$ vertices these are equivalent: it is a tree; there is exactly one path between any two vertices; it is connected with $n - 1$ edges; it has no cycles and $n - 1$ edges. Every tree with at least $2$ vertices has at least $2$ leaves (vertices of degree $1$).

Why $n - 1$ edges? Take a longest path in the tree; its end has degree $1$, because any other edge there would either extend the path or close a cycle. So every tree has a leaf. Remove a leaf and its edge: what remains is still connected with no cycles, a tree with one vertex fewer and one edge fewer. Repeat until one vertex and $0$ edges remain. Each step removed one vertex and one edge, so the original had exactly one edge fewer than vertices. Adding any edge to a tree joins two vertices that already had a path between them, so it creates exactly one cycle.

blocks.title: Counting edges
blocks.q: A tree has $25$ vertices. How many edges? A forest (a graph with no cycles) has $25$ vertices and $4$ components. How many edges?
steps: Tree: $25 - 1 = 24$ edges.
Forest: each component is a tree with one edge fewer than vertices; over $4$ trees that is $25 - 4 = 21$ edges.

blocks.title: Counting leaves
blocks.q: A tree has $3$ vertices of degree $3$, $1$ vertex of degree $4$, and every other vertex is a leaf. How many leaves?
steps: Let $\ell$ be the number of leaves. Then $v = 4 + \ell$ and $e = v - 1 = 3 + \ell$.
Handshake: $3 \cdot 3 + 4 + \ell = 2(3 + \ell)$, so $13 + \ell = 6 + 2\ell$ and $\ell = 7$.
Shortcut: $\ell = 2 + \sum (d - 2)$ over the vertices with $d \ge 3$: $2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 7$.

blocks.html: Calling any graph with $n - 1$ edges a tree. A triangle plus one separate vertex has $4$ vertices and $3$ edges, yet it has a cycle and is not connected. The edge count is a test only together with "connected" or "no cycles." Check both conditions, or use one of them plus the count.

blocks.html: Suppose towns must be linked by roads, each possible road has a cost, and every town must be reachable. The cheapest network has no cycles (a cycle always has a removable road), so it is one of the trees inside the graph. Finding the cheapest one is easy, by a greedy rule.

A spanning tree of a connected graph is a tree that uses all of its vertices; with $n$ vertices it has $n - 1$ edges. In a weighted graph, a minimum spanning tree has the least total weight. Kruskal's algorithm: go through the edges from cheapest to most expensive, and add each edge unless it would close a cycle with the edges already chosen; stop at $n - 1$ edges.

Why does greed not backfire? Split the vertices into any two groups. The cheapest edge crossing between the groups belongs to some minimum spanning tree: if a tree avoided it, adding it would create a cycle that crosses the split somewhere else, at an edge at least as expensive, and swapping the two edges would not raise the cost. Every edge Kruskal adds is the cheapest crossing between the component it joins and the rest, so it never makes a choice it regrets. Skipping cycle-closing edges is what keeps the result a tree.

blocks.title: Running Kruskal's algorithm
blocks.q: For the graph above (weights: $DF\,1$, $BE\,2$, $AC\,3$, $AB\,4$, $BC\,5$, $BD\,6$, $CE\,7$, $DE\,8$, $EF\,9$), find a minimum spanning tree.

$BC$ ($5$): $B$ and $C$ are already connected through $A$, so it would close the cycle $B - A - C - B$. Skip.
$BD$ ($6$): joins $\{D, F\}$ to the rest. Add. That is $5 = 6 - 1$ edges: stop.
Total weight $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 16$.

And a "tree" with fewer than $n - 1$ edges does not reach every vertex. Check: before adding an edge, ask whether its ends are already connected; at the end, count $n - 1$ edges.
Prim's algorithm grows a single tree instead: start at any vertex, and repeatedly add the cheapest edge with exactly one end in the tree. It finds a minimum spanning tree too.

blocks.html: A map app finds the fastest route among millions of roads in an instant. The core idea is Dijkstra's algorithm, which grows a set of vertices whose distances are known for sure. Like Kruskal's algorithm, it makes one greedy choice per round, but a different one.

Dijkstra's algorithm (weights $\ge 0$): give the start distance $0$ and every other vertex $\infty$. Each round, settle the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance; then, for each neighbor, if going through the settled vertex is shorter, lower that neighbor's tentative distance. A vertex's distance is final only when it is settled.

Why is the closest unsettled vertex $u$ safe to settle? Any other route from the start to $u$ must leave the settled set at some point, through an edge to some unsettled vertex $w$. Reaching $w$ already costs at least its tentative distance, which is at least $u$'s (that is how $u$ was chosen), and the rest of the route adds weights that are $\ge 0$. So no route beats $u$'s current distance. This is also why negative weights break the algorithm: a later negative edge could make a detour cheaper.

blocks.title: A full run
blocks.q: In the graph above, find the shortest distance from $A$ to every vertex.
steps: Settle $A$ ($0$). Update: $B = 4$, $C = 2$.
Settle $C$ ($2$, the smallest). Update: $B = \min(4, 2 + 1) = 3$; $E = 2 + 8 = 10$.
Settle $B$ ($3$). Update: $D = 3 + 5 = 8$; $E$ stays $10$ ($3 + 10 = 13$ is worse).
Settle $E$ ($10$). Update: $F = \min(14, 10 + 3) = 13$. Settle $F$ ($13$).

blocks.title: The first route found is not always the best
blocks.q: In the run above, $B$ was first reached with distance $4$. Why wasn't $B$ settled then?
steps: When $B$ got its tentative $4$ from $A$, $C$ was closer ($2$).
Settling $C$ first revealed the route $A \to C \to B$ of length $3$.
Settling only the closest vertex each round is what guarantees each settled distance is final.

blocks.html: Settling a vertex as soon as it is reached. If $B$ had been fixed at $4$, every distance computed through $B$ would be off too. Check: each round, compare all unsettled tentative distances and settle only the smallest; until then, a distance is just the best found so far.

blocks.html: Scheduling exams so that no student has two at once, assigning radio frequencies so that neighbors don't interfere, coloring a map: each is coloring the vertices of a graph. It uses cycles and the special graphs, especially bipartite ones.

A proper coloring gives each vertex a color so that joined vertices get different colors. The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the fewest colors that work. $\chi(K_{n}) = n$; $\chi(C_{n}) = 2$ for even $n$ and $3$ for odd $n$; and a graph with at least one edge has $\chi(G) = 2$ exactly when it has no cycle of odd length (it is bipartite).

Going around a cycle, two colors must alternate. Around an even cycle that works; around an odd cycle the last vertex ends up next to a vertex of its own color. So any odd cycle forces a third color. Conversely, if there is no odd cycle, color a starting vertex red, its neighbors blue, their neighbors red, and so on outward; a clash would mean two routes of different parity between the same vertices, which together contain an odd cycle. To show $\chi(G) = k$, you always need two things: a coloring with $k$ colors, and a reason $k - 1$ is not enough.

blocks.title: A wheel
blocks.q: A wheel has a 5-cycle rim and a hub joined to all five rim vertices. Find its chromatic number.
steps: The rim is an odd cycle, so it needs $3$ colors.
The hub is joined to every rim vertex, so it cannot reuse any rim color: a $4$th color.
Four colors suffice (three on the rim, one on the hub), so $\chi = 4$.

blocks.title: Scheduling exams
blocks.q: Exams A–E: A conflicts with B and C; B with C and D; D with E. How many time slots are needed?
steps: Vertices are exams, edges are conflicts, slots are colors.
$A$, $B$, $C$ form a triangle, so at least $3$ slots.
Three work: slot 1: $A, D$; slot 2: $B, E$; slot 3: $C$. Check every conflict: no edge joins two exams in one slot.

blocks.title: Greedy coloring depends on order
blocks.q: The path $a - b - c - d$ is colored greedily in the order $a, d, b, c$: each vertex takes the lowest-numbered color not used by its colored neighbors. How many colors are used?
steps: $a$ gets $1$. $d$ gets $1$ (no colored neighbors yet).
$b$ is next to $a$ (color $1$), so it gets $2$. $c$ is next to $b$ ($2$) and $d$ ($1$), so it gets $3$.
Three colors, although the path is bipartite and $2$ colors suffice (order $a, b, c, d$ gives $1, 2, 1, 2$).

blocks.html: Trusting a greedy coloring to be optimal. Greedy coloring is fast and never uses more than one color beyond the largest degree, but the number it uses depends on the order of the vertices, as the path example shows. Check: a coloring only gives an upper bound; to know $\chi(G)$, also find a reason fewer colors fail, such as an odd cycle or a group of vertices all joined to each other.

blocks.html: A circuit board cannot let wires cross, and a map's borders never cross. Graphs that can be drawn without crossing edges obey a remarkable formula, proved by building up from a spanning tree one edge at a time.

A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane with no edges crossing. Such a drawing splits the plane into faces, including the unbounded outside face. Euler's formula: for a connected planar drawing, $$v - e + f = 2.$$ Consequences: a simple planar graph with $v \ge 3$ vertices has $e \le 3v - 6$, and if it has no triangles, $e \le 2v - 4$. So $K_{5}$ and $K_{3,3}$ are not planar.

Start with a spanning tree of the drawing: $v$ vertices, $v - 1$ edges, and one face (a tree encloses no region), so $v - e + f = v - (v - 1) + 1 = 2$. Now add the remaining edges one at a time. Each new edge runs through some face and splits it in two, so $e$ and $f$ both go up by $1$, and $v - e + f$ stays $2$. For the bound: every face is bordered by at least $3$ edges and every edge borders at most $2$ faces, so $3f \le 2e$; substituting $f = 2 - v + e$ gives $e \le 3v - 6$.

blocks.cap: $K_{4}$ drawn with a crossing. Drag a vertex to remove it; once there are no crossings, the faces are shaded and the readout checks $v - e + f$.

blocks.title: The cube
blocks.q: The cube graph is planar (draw a small square inside a large one and join matching corners). Check Euler's formula.
steps: The drawing has $5$ bounded faces (the small square and four side regions) plus the outside: $f = 6$, one per face of the cube.

blocks.title: $K_{5}$ is not planar
blocks.q: Use the edge bound to show that $K_{5}$ is not planar.
steps: A simple planar graph with $5$ vertices has at most $3 \cdot 5 - 6 = 9$ edges.
$10 > 9$, so $K_{5}$ cannot be planar.

blocks.title: $K_{3,3}$ is not planar
blocks.q: $K_{3,3}$ has $9$ edges and $6$ vertices, and $9 \le 3 \cdot 6 - 6 = 12$. Why is it still not planar?
steps: The bound $e \le 3v - 6$ passes, so it decides nothing.
$K_{3,3}$ is bipartite, so it has no triangles; every face would need at least $4$ edges, giving $e \le 2v - 4 = 8$.
$9 > 8$, so it is not planar.

blocks.html: Forgetting the outside face, or using the bound to prove planarity. Counting only the enclosed regions of the cube drawing gives $f = 5$ and $8 - 12 + 5 = 1$. And "$e \le 3v - 6$, so it is planar" is wrong: $K_{3,3}$ passes that test. Check: always count the unbounded face; the edge bounds can only show a graph is not planar.
